analysis.one_liner: Makes it much harder to sue large companies as a group and forces asbestos trusts to expose claimants' files.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 220-201 on March 9, 2017, with 220 of 236 Republicans in favor and no Democrats, but the Senate never voted on it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the rules for class action lawsuits in federal court. It would bar courts from approving many class actions unless every single member of the class had the same type and scope of injury, cap and delay lawyers' fees, freeze evidence-gathering while dismissal motions are pending, and require plaintiffs in big consolidated injury cases to prove their claims with medical records within 45 days or lose. It would also require asbestos bankruptcy trusts to publish quarterly reports naming claimants and describing their exposure history, which defendants could then use against them in court.
analysis.who_benefits: Large companies facing class action lawsuits over defective products, drugs, financial misconduct, and other harms. The bill would make it far harder for harmed consumers to combine their small claims into one case, forcing most to sue alone or not at all, and it would give asbestos defendants access to trust claim data they could use to dispute injury claims.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Big corporate defendants and their insurers

how_it_helps.text: No federal court could certify a class action for money damages unless the party suing shows every proposed class member suffered the same type and scope of injury as the named representatives — a requirement that would disqualify most consumer and injury class actions, where harm varies person to person [S3][S5].

The bill would freeze evidence gathering (discovery) while early motions to dismiss are pending, so defendants could postpone revealing internal documents until after a judge has decided whether the case can even proceed [S3].

Lawyers' fees could not be paid until all money was distributed to class members and could never exceed what class members actually received, sharply reducing the economics of taking on complex corporate cases [S3].

The asbestos title requires bankruptcy trusts to file quarterly public reports describing every claim demand, including the claimant's name and exposure history, and to turn over payment information to any party litigating asbestos liability [S4][S5].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers, patients, and workers hurt by corporate wrongdoing. Because each person's individual loss is often too small to justify a solo lawsuit, the bill's restrictions would mean many valid injuries go unredressed, and companies would face less legal risk for selling dangerous products.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers and workers with injury claims

drawbacks.text: Genuine problems exist in class action practice: lawyers have sometimes collected fees worth more than class members received, and some mass tort claims have lacked solid medical evidence, so disclosure and proof requirements respond to a real concern [S3][S4].

The uniform-injury requirement goes far beyond targeting abuse: making every class member's injury identical would end most group litigation for small-dollar harms entirely, leaving individuals no practical way to recover [S3].

The asbestos trust reporting would expose claimants' names and exposure histories on public dockets, handing defendant companies detailed ammunition to challenge sick claimants' compensation while giving them nothing in return [S4][S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some transparency provisions — fee accounting reports, disclosure of lawyers' financial stakes, and third-party funding disclosure — are reasonable anti-abuse measures. But the bill's core is a near-ban on consumer and injury class actions: the same-type-and-scope-of-injury rule plus the evidence requirements and fee limits would eliminate group lawsuits as a practical tool, and the asbestos disclosure rules impose real privacy harm on sick people with no compensating benefit to them. On balance, the costs fall almost entirely on ordinary people while the benefits accrue to corporate defendants.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it in March 2017 on a near party-line vote, but the Senate referred it to its Judiciary Committee and never brought it to a vote, so the bill died when that Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Introduced February 9, 2017 by Rep. Bob Goodlatte, the bill cleared the House Judiciary Committee, which reported it 19-12 on March 7, 2017 [S7].

On March 9, 2017, Democrats offered a series of amendments on the House floor, including exemptions for drinking water and other consumer protections; every one was defeated, and a motion to send the bill back with an exemption for drinking water lawsuits failed 188-234, with all but one Republican voting no [S7][S8].
The House passed the bill 220-201 with one member voting present: 220 of 236 Republicans in favor (14 defections) and 0 of 193 Democrats in favor [S9].
The Senate received the bill on March 13, 2017 and referred it to the Judiciary Committee, where it sat with no further action through the end of the 115th Congress [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary consumers, workers, and asbestos victims are better off, because their ability to sue companies as a group was left intact. Large corporate defendants avoided these new shields but also continue operating under current law, which they had sought to change.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured consumers kept their right to group lawsuits

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split almost entirely by party: 220 of 236 Republicans voted yes (14 broke ranks) while none of the 193 Democrats did; the motion to recommit was nearly the mirror image, with 187 Democrats and 1 Republican in favor [S8][S9].

industries.industry: Corporate defendants (consumer products, drugs, finance, other companies facing class suits)
industries.note: The uniform-injury rule, discovery freeze, fee limits, and stricter federal-court routing would make group lawsuits far harder to bring and win, cutting companies' legal exposure and settlement payouts. Ordinary people injured by corporate conduct would bear that cost directly [S3][S5].

industries.industry: Asbestos defendant companies and their insurers
industries.note: The FACT Act would force asbestos trusts to publish claimant names, exposure histories, and payment data that defendants could use to contest or reduce injury claims. The information flows one way — to the companies facing liability — while sick claimants' medical and exposure histories become public [S4][S5].

Fee caps, delayed payment, mandatory accountings, and certification barriers would shrink both the number of viable cases and the fees available. Because this bar works by bundling many small claims, the industry's interest in the bill runs alongside ordinary claimants' [S3][S5].
